# Underscore: implicit values and wildcards

The exact identifier `_` has several context-dependent roles in Edva. It can
be an implicit function parameter, a cycle item, a branch payload, or a pattern
wildcard. Its spelling alone does not tell you which role applies.

| Context | Meaning of `_` |
|---|---|
| `(_ * 2)` | Parameter of a grouped implicit lambda |
| `(* 2)` | Parameter inserted by operator-section syntax |
| Implicit cycle body | Current item |
| Bare ram payload branch | Payload of the selected slot |
| Omitted choice subject | Existing implicit value being tested |
| Structured pattern, such as `(a = _, b = 20)` | Match without binding that component |
| `_ = expression` | Forbidden assignment target (E2044); call functions directly to discard results |
| `_ => expression` | Forbidden explicit parameter declaration |
| `_name`, `__`, `_i` | Different identifiers; `_i` additionally has a cycle role |

These roles share syntax and have strict, consistent scoping and typing rules.
The [consistency review](#consistency-review) below summarizes the resolved
contracts and compiler guarantees.

## Identifiers and literal text

An underscore can begin or occur within an ordinary identifier. Only the exact
name `_` has the special parameter restriction:

```{.dva .run}
#use io

_value = 4
__ = 5
increment = _arg => _arg + 1

io::out(increment(_value))
io::out(__)
// => 5
// => 5
```

Names beginning with `_` do not acquire privacy or discard semantics merely
from that spelling. A prime-suffixed identifier follows the ordinary mutable
binding rules; it is not the exact identifier `_`.

Inside a String or Rune literal, `_` is literal text. It is not a numeric
separator: spell one thousand as `1000`, not `1_000`. The compiler rejects
underscores in integer and float literals (`1_000`, `1_000.5`) with E1019.

## Grouped implicit-parameter lambdas

A grouped expression containing a free `_` becomes a function with **one**
implicit parameter. Repeated references use that same argument:

```{.dva .run}
#use io

identity = (_)
square = (_ * _)
subtract_from_ten = (10 - _)

io::out(identity(7))
io::out(square(4))
io::out(subtract_from_ten(2))
// => 7
// => 16
// => 8
```

This is not an automatically numbered argument list: `(_ + _)` does not
accept two separate arguments. Use `left, right => left + right` for that.
The implicit parameter's type follows the ordinary function inference rules;
it is not inherently Int.

### Call delimiters versus grouping

The parentheses of `f(_)` delimit call arguments. In a context where `_`
already names a value, this calls `f` with that value. To make a callback
which calls `f`, group the whole expression: `(f(_))`.

Similarly, `io::out $ _` uses the current implicit value, while
`(io::out $ _)` creates an implicit lambda. A cycle can consume that lambda
as its body:

```{.dva .run}
#use io

3 @ (io::out $ _)
// => 0
// => 1
// => 2
```

### Inner groups bind first

`(_ * 2 + 3)` has one implicit parameter. By contrast,
`(3 - 2 * (_ + 1))` first creates a function from `(_ + 1)`; the outer
expression then attempts arithmetic on that function. Write a named lambda
when grouping a compound calculation would otherwise create an inner lambda:
`value => 3 - 2 * (value + 1)`.

The transformation is syntactic. Even when an outer `_` already exists,
`(_ + 1)` creates a new parameter rather than just grouping the outer value:

```{.dva .run}
#use io

7..8 @
   increment = (_ + 1)
   io::out(increment(3))
// => 4
```

A differently named inner lambda does not itself bind `_`. This permits an
outer implicit parameter captured by that inner lambda:

```{.dva .run}
#use io

make_adder: Int => (Int => Int)
make_adder = (value => _ + value)

add_ten = make_adder(10)
io::out(add_ten(3))
// => 13
```

For readers, the explicit equivalent `base => value => base + value` is often
easier to follow.

### Record literals need an enclosing group

The parentheses in `(a = _, b = 1)` construct a record; they do not by
themselves create an implicit lambda. A surrounding group supplies that role:

```{.dva .run}
#use io

make_pair: Int => (a: Int, b: Int)
make_pair = ((a = _, b = 1))

pair = make_pair(4)
io::out(pair.a)
io::out(pair.b)
// => 4
// => 1
```

The same distinction matters when deciding which syntax introduces a grouping
expression rather than an argument list, record, or pattern.

## Operator sections

An [operator section](operator-sections.qmd) inserts `_` without writing it:

```{.dva .run}
#use io

double = * 2
square = * _
io::out(double(6))
io::out(square(4))
// => 12
// => 16
```

`* 2` is equivalent to `(_ * 2)`. In `* _`, the written `_` is another
reference to the section's same parameter, giving `(_ * _)`. It does not
create an additional argument.

Sections have their own allowed-operator set and right-hand-expression boundary.
Those rules do not apply to arbitrary grouped lambdas such as `(_ != 0)`.

## Cycles: `_` and `_i`

In an implicit cycle body, `_` is the current item. For an integer range,
`_i` is the zero-based iteration index, which can differ from the item:

```{.dva .run}
#use io

10..12 @
   io::out $ _
   io::out $ _i
// => 10
// => 0
// => 11
// => 1
```

Arrays and slices supply elements; normal String cycles supply byte values.
`_i` is an index for those sequential iterables. It is a distinct name:
grouping `(_i)` alone does not create an implicit lambda. In `(_ + _i)`
inside a cycle, `_` becomes the lambda's parameter and `_i` is captured
from the enclosing cycle.

The implementation also makes implicit aliases available in named cycle
bodies, and properly restores enclosing bindings across nesting:

```{.dva .run}
#use io

10..11 @
   io::out $ _
   1 @ io::out $ _
   io::out $ _
// => 10
// => 0
// => 10
// => 11
// => 0
// => 11
```

Nested cycles preserve outer values by saving and restoring `_` and `_i` at cycle entry and exit.

Implicit cycle variables `_` and `_i` do not survive cycle exit: reading `_i` after a cycle finishes or after an early break is rejected at compile time with `E3004: Undefined: _i`. If a loop index must persist after loop termination (such as a scan position in a String cycle), declare an explicit named cycle index (`text @ b, index =>`).

### Maps use a key, not a sequential index

Map cycles have value/key roles. Their lowering uses `_` for the value and
`_i` for the key, whose type reflects the actual map key type (for example,
`String` for `String ^ Int`):

```{.dva .run}
#use io

#type Values String ^ Int
values = Values()
values ^ "key" = 7

values @
   io::out $ _
   io::out $ _i
// => 7
// => key
```

## Ramification payloads

In a bare branch handling a payload, `_` denotes that selected slot's value.
It can extract the payload unchanged or participate in an expression:

```{.dva .run}
#use io

r: < Int | >
r = <+ 5 +>

value = r | _ | 0
increased = r | _ + 2 | 0
io::out(value)
io::out(increased)
// => 5
// => 7
```

A negative slot with a payload has the same role, using its own payload type:

```{.dva .run}
#use io

#type Result < Int | Int >
r = Result(<- 7 +>)
value: Int
value = r | _ + 1 | _ + 2
io::out(value)
// => 9
```

Do not confuse a negative payload with a unit/absence slot. For `< Int | >`,
the second slot has no integer payload: extracting `_` from an absent unit slot
(`r | _ | _`) is rejected at compile time with `E3004: Undefined: _`. Always
supply an explicit default expression (such as `r | _ | 0`).

### Error extraction is special

For a result with a negative `Error` payload, bare `_` extraction of that slot
uses the fatal-error behavior. The common `result | _ | _` spelling therefore
does not merely discard or innocently forward every possible error.

For example, an array index read returns an element or Error. This succeeds:

```{.dva .run}
#use io

values = Int{}
values += 42
value = values(0) | _ | _
io::out(value)
// => 42
```

The same extraction from index 0 of an empty array terminates with E4011.
Use a named negative branch to inspect a recoverable Error, as described in
[Error](../types/error.qmd), or use `!!` when fatal extraction is intended.

### Parentheses around payload expressions

The free-underscore scan is binder-aware: payload-bearing branches (`Bare`, `Variant`)
bind `_` within their branch body. Grouping an expression containing payload arithmetic,
such as `(r | _ + 2 | 0)`, produces a normal value expression rather than converting
the grouped choice into an implicit lambda:

```{.dva .run}
#use io

r: < Int | >
r = <+ 5 +>
x = (r | _ + 2 | 0)
io::out(x)
// => 7
```

## Choice predicates and omitted subjects

In a grouped predicate, `_` is the predicate function's argument, supplied by
the choice subject:

```{.dva .run}
#use io

label = 7 [(_ > 0 && _ < 10)] "single digit" | "other"
io::out(label)
// => single digit
```

An omitted choice subject uses the current `_`. This can be an existing cycle
item, or the argument introduced by grouping the choice:

```{.dva .run}
#use io

sign = ([< 0] -1 | 1)
io::out(sign(-2))
io::out(sign(2))

0..2 @
   [0] io::out("zero")
   | io::out("other")
// => -1
// => 1
// => zero
// => other
```

An omitted subject without an enclosing implicit value is rejected with
E3003. It does not mean “reuse the previous expression's result.”

Ordinary value and predicate choices (`7 [> 0] ... | 0`) test conditions on a subject
rather than extracting a payload from a container. They do not bind `_` in their branch
bodies; referencing `_` in an ordinary guarded branch (such as `7 [> 0] _ + 2 | 0`)
is rejected with `E3004: Undefined: _`. To use the subject, bind it explicitly with a
named function parameter (`x => x [> 0] x + 2 | 0`).

This behavior also preserves function-valued branches in ordinary choices, such as
selecting operator sections:

```{.dva .run}
#use io

choose_transform: Int => (Int => Int)
choose_transform = mode =>
   mode [> 0] (* 2) | (+ 1)

transform = choose_transform(1)
io::out(transform(7))
// => 14
```

## Wildcards in structured patterns

In a parsed pattern, `_` matches a component without naming it. Other parts
of the pattern still constrain the match:

```{.dva .run}
#use io

#type Pair (a: Int, b: Int)
pair = Pair(10, 20)
label = pair [(a = _, b = 20)] "matched" | "other"
io::out(label)

#type Box < Item(Int), Empty >
box = Box(Item, 3)
kind = box [Item _] "item" | "empty"
io::out(kind)
// => matched
// => item
```

Nested patterns can use the same wildcard, for example `[Mul (_, Lit 0)]`.
Each wildcard independently ignores its component. Repeated `_` patterns do
not assert equality between components, and a wildcard does not introduce a
value binding for the branch body to read.

Bare `[_]` is **not** a general wildcard guard. It takes the expression/value
guard path, not the structured-pattern wildcard path. With no existing `_`,
the tested `7 [_]` did not match, while `0 [_]` did. Use the ordinary bare
fallback `| result` for a catch-all branch.

Likewise, `(a, _) = ...` is not supported destructuring-assignment syntax.
Pattern matching and record construction are different contexts.

## Assignment to `_` and ignored results

Assigning to `_` (`_ = ...`, `_ := ...`, `_ ::= ...`) is forbidden (E2044).
It cannot be used as an assignment target:

```{.dva expected-error="E2044"}
_ = 7
```

To call a function for its effects, use a bare call statement directly when its API and
the surrounding construct allow that. If its result matters, bind it to a
descriptive name. Do not use `_ = ...` to mean error handling: assigning a
result does not inspect or propagate its error slot.

## Forbidden explicit parameters and unavailable values

An explicit parameter named exactly `_` is rejected in ordinary functions,
multi-parameter functions, named cycle binders, and branch lambdas:

```{.dva expected-error="E2040"}
f = _ => 42
```

The restriction also covers explicit compile-time parameters. Use a name such
as `ignored` when a callable must accept an unused argument. For a branch that
just returns a constant, write the constant without introducing a function.
Names such as `_arg`, `__`, and `_i` remain legal explicit parameter names.

### Undefined implicit value references

Outside a supported implicit-binding context, `_` cannot be read as a value. The compiler rejects unbound value references (`x = _`, `value => _ + 1`) with `E3004: Undefined: _`. `_` is not an automatic alias for explicitly named function parameters, nor does it synthesize a default zero value:

```{.dva expected-error="E3004"}
x: Int
x = _
```

## Consistency review

The underscore scoping and typing contracts are specified and enforced as follows:

| Area | Contract and resolution | Diagnostic |
|---|---|---|
| Name resolution | Unbound references (`x = _`, `value => _ + 1`) are rejected; omitted choice subjects without enclosing `_` are rejected | `E3004` / `E3003` |
| Discard idiom | Assignment to `_` (`_ = ...`, `_ := ...`, `_ ::= ...`) is forbidden; bare call statements are used directly | `E2044` |
| Grouping | Payload-bearing branches (`Bare`, `Variant`) are recognized as bound; grouped arithmetic payload branches `(r | _ + 2 | 0)` evaluate to values | Validated |
| Branch subjects | Ordinary value and predicate choices do not bind `_` in branch bodies, preserving function-valued branches | `E3004` on unbound `_` |
| Nested cycles | Inner cycles save and restore outer implicit item `_` and index `_i` bindings upon completion | Validated |
| Cycle indices | Implicit index `_i` does not survive cycle exit; post-cycle reads are rejected | `E3004` |
| Map keys | Implicit key `_i` is typed with the map's actual key type (`m.key`) | Validated |
| Absent payloads | Payload extraction from absent unit slots (`< Int | >` negative slot or payload-free enum variant) is rejected | `E3004` |
| Numeric separators | Underscore numeric separators (`1_000`, `1_000.5`) are rejected | `E1019` |

Other distinctions remain standard syntax rules: `_` in a pattern is a wildcard, not an expression; a grouped implicit lambda introduces one parameter; and `_i` is an identifier with cycle index semantics.

The [detailed review and reproductions](../../../audits/2026-10-14-underscore/report.md) record the original audit baseline and rerun probe results.
